rv.q: Strongly dappled as it is by images of illness and mortality, “Marvin’s Room” still shines with vital, quirky life.
Anne Kauffman's luminous revival for the Roundabout tends to McPherson's legacy with grace.
But it is somehow, also, fatally mild.
'Marvin's Room' is a thickly sugared pill, glib and sentimental to a fault.
A play that resonated deeply back in its day ends up now gasping for oxygen on a stage full of dead air.
Unfortunately, this first Broadway production of Marvin’s Roomnever quite justifies its trip back to the early ’90s.

The new Broadway revival, now playing at the Theatre and superbly directed by Anne Kauffman, does "Marvin's Room" extraordinary justice -- it makes the case that a mostly forgotten play might just be a modern classic.
But this is still that play in which everyone ends up married and nobody wins.
Marvin’s Room is certainly a room to visit.
Zany, morbid, and brimful of compassion, Marvin’s Room is the defining work of a playwright who died of complications from AIDS at the age of 33.
A most gentle and obviously personal story of the power of love to transcend life's dark turns.
McPherson had a keen sense of family dynamics and the need for pitch-black humor in the face of tragedy—a balance that's finely maintained in the hands of director Anne Kauffman in this revival

"So much is so sad in the lives of Bessie and Lee as to make the audience fully justified in wondering: Should we be laughing at this? Yet laugh we do, thanks to the playwright’s subversive worldview, and a production directed with unflashy effectiveness by Kauffman.
Lili Taylor and Janeane Garofalo are sisters reunited by illness in the gratifying and affecting Broadway premiere of 'Marvin's Room.'
The brief candle of his great talent shines in the belated Broadway premiere of Marvin's Room, notwithstanding the design and staging miscalculation noted here.
Even if all the comic business still landed throughout instead of rather sporadically, it's not as a comedy that Marvin's Room survives but as a very human look at life, love and death.
While the acting is fine, the comedic elements of the story about the intertwining of life and death sometimes feel forced.
In the end, despite the incongruities between the production and the play itself, Marvin's Room resonates with beautiful insights into the ways we approach the end of life.

A cute sense of humor pops up throughout the play, such as when Ruth dresses up for a special episode of her favorite television soap opera, Lee shamelessly dumps a tray of candy into her purse while touring a nursing home and Bessie is rescued at Disney World by a costumed cartoon character.
Under the direction of Anne Kauffman it's given a fairly ho-hum Broadway debut.
A work that could have succumbed to all sorts of excess miraculously never puts a foot wrong.
McPherson whimsically juggles the real and the unreal, the sick and the inane.
But what strikes me most about Marvin’s Room is its perceptiveness about the sick, about how we treat them and how they feel about it.
On close inspection, McPherson’s play delivers a defiantly positive prognoses.
All the choices in this tender revival reveal an involving and human story, unmarred by overdrawn theatrics.
Marvin’s Room will be a rewarding place to be this summer.

Marvin’s Room is a tragicomic story that boldly addresses the question of what happens when a caregiver needs a caregiver as well as a bittersweet reminder of the weight of family responsibility and heartbreaking loss.
"Marvin's Room" is not a classic, but it is an often touching and funny drama that explores the bonds of family and honors the caretakers who sacrifice part of themselves to serve the ones they love.
But it still works, and thanks largely to the cast, it is at times incredibly powerful.
It’s an intimate story that seems a bit lost in the vastness of the Theatre.
If you want your foundations shaken, look elsewhere.
A tasty stew of family drama. Though I prefer my drama with a bit more spice.
The design, it seems, is not a gift given to the actors or the production, it is more the culprit and a vast one.
Although an often touching play, this mostly reverent revival of Scott McPherson’s Marvin’s Room never fully envelops you.
After the nursing home scene, though, and for the rest of the play, Kauffman and the cast smartly probe the play’s depths, and the final few scenes are quite moving.
The current Broadway revival however, doesn’t say it as well as it could.
Two hours-plus, however, are simply too long to wait while these questions are answered.
It almost makes you forget how disappointing this current revival of an otherwise moving play is.
The characters never ring true, however.
While it may have augured well for its creator, who died in 1992 at age 33 after receiving several major awards, it seems to have lost much of its vigor in the intervening decades.
It's a touching play (Scott McPherson) but this incarnation left me feeling empty and un-touched.

"The play itself seems outdated and tame...The acting is uniformly good, but if you have seen the film version...it is hard to not compare. This is not the tearjerker the film was. As a matter of fact, the show barely manages to elicit much emotion at all. Anne Kauffman has under-directed this piece.
I spent most of the evening wondering why this off-Broadway play was revived in the first place.
